planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines on a trellis in full sun once soil can be worked in spring.

directions: Chardonel was bred at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva by crossing the French-American hybrid Seyval with Chardonnay, pairing Chardonnay-like wine quality with far better winter hardiness and vine health than straight vinifera. It ripens mid-to-late season into large, productive clusters of green-gold berries, so thin crop loads on young vines to avoid overbearing. Train on a vertical shoot-positioned trellis and prune to short spurs; it tolerates the cold winters of the Northeast and Midwest noticeably better than its Chardonnay parent.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — Grape Varieties

common_name: Aromella Grape (Cornell-Bred Aromatic Cold-Hardy White Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines on a trellis in full sun once soil can be worked in spring.

directions: Aromella was released in 2013 by Cornell's grape breeding program at Geneva, New York, a cross of Traminette and Ravat 34 selected for a distinctly floral, Muscat-like aromatic character while retaining strong cold hardiness for Northeastern vineyards. Clusters are medium-sized and ripen in early-to-mid season, making this a good choice where a long, hot ripening window for aromatic vinifera types isn't reliable. Give it a vertical shoot-positioned trellis, full sun, and winter protection of the trunk in zone 5 plantings, and manage canopy density to keep its thin-skinned berries free of bunch rot.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — Grape Varieties

common_name: Arandell Grape (Cornell-Bred Fungus-Resistant Red Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines on a trellis in full sun once soil can be worked in spring.

directions: Arandell came out of Bruce Reisch's no-spray breeding program at Cornell's Geneva campus, bred specifically to cut fungicide needs by showing strong field resistance to powdery mildew, which lets low-input and home growers trim much of the spray schedule straight vinifera reds demand. It produces medium clusters of dark berries that make a solid, fruity red wine, ripening mid-season on vigorous, cold-hardy vines suited to Northeastern winters. Train to a vertical shoot-positioned trellis, keep the canopy open for air movement, and still scout for disease in wet years since resistance reduces but doesn't eliminate spray needs.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — Grape Varieties

common_name: Worden Grape (Early-Ripening Concord-Type Table and Juice Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines on a trellis or arbor in full sun once soil can be worked in spring.

directions: Worden arose in 1863 as an open-pollinated Concord seedling raised by Schuyler Worden, an early settler of Minetto, New York, and has stayed in home-garden cultivation because it ripens roughly a week ahead of Concord with larger berries and a similar slip-skin flavor. Clusters are loose-to-medium and the vine is vigorous and productive, making it a forgiving choice for a backyard arbor. Prune hard each winter on a cane- or spur-pruning system and thin crowded shoots in summer to let light reach developing clusters and improve sugar and color at harvest.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — Grape Varieties
University of Minnesota Extension — Grape Growing

common_name: Agawam Grape (Historic Self-Fertile Rogers Hybrid Red Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines on a trellis or arbor in full sun once soil can be worked in spring.

directions: Agawam, also sold as Rogers 15, was one of the dozens of labrusca-vinifera hybrids E.S. Rogers raised in Salem, Massachusetts in the mid-1800s, and it stands out among that family as reliably self-fertile, so a single home vine will set fruit without a pollinizer. The large, reddish-brown berries ripen in a loose cluster with a rich, somewhat spicy labrusca flavor good for fresh eating. Give it full sun, a sturdy trellis, and dormant-season pruning to spurs; it is winter-hardy enough for most of the Northeast and upper Midwest without special protection.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — Grape Varieties
University of Minnesota Extension — Grape Growing

common_name: Brighton Grape (Historic Early-Ripening Red Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines on a trellis or arbor in full sun once soil can be worked in spring.

directions: Brighton was raised by nurseryman Jacob Moore in Brighton, New York, near Rochester, around 1870 and remained a favorite dooryard grape for decades on the strength of its early ripening and attractive red-to-coppery berries with a sweet, mild labrusca flavor. Vines are moderately vigorous and best cropped lightly, since overloaded clusters can struggle to size up evenly compared with Concord. Plant it on a trellis in full sun, prune to spurs each winter, and pick as soon as berries color fully, since Brighton does not hold quality long on the vine once ripe.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — Grape Varieties

common_name: Van Buren Grape (Extra-Early Cold-Hardy Concord-Type Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines on a trellis or arbor in full sun once soil can be worked in spring.

directions: Van Buren was released in 1935 from the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station's grape breeding work at Geneva, a cross of Fredonia and Worden aimed at beating Concord to ripeness, and it reliably colors and sweetens weeks earlier, making it useful for short-season northern gardens. Berries are blue-black with the classic slip-skin labrusca flavor, borne on compact, winter-hardy vines that tolerate colder sites than many Concord-type grapes. Train on a trellis in full sun, prune to spurs in late winter, and expect a productive, low-fuss dooryard vine once established.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — Grape Varieties

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines on a trellis or arbor in full sun once soil can be worked in spring.

directions: Isabella is an early-1800s American hybrid of Vitis labrusca and a Vitis vinifera parent that proved unusually tolerant of heat and humidity for its era, which carried it far beyond its origins into near-ubiquitous dooryard and small-vineyard planting across Brazil, the Andes, and other warm, humid regions where many pure vinifera grapes struggle. Its slip-skin, dark purple berries have the classic musky-sweet labrusca flavor and serve equally well for fresh eating, juice, or simple home winemaking. Give it a sturdy trellis in full sun and well-drained soil, prune to spurs or canes each winter, and expect good vigor and disease tolerance with minimal spraying compared to fine wine vinifera.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences — Grape Varieties
